title: What sanctions compliance training does OFAC expect from US financial institutions?
description: OFAC's 2019 compliance Framework makes training one of five program components: at least annual, role-based and assessed. Explained as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: The US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) expects sanctions compliance training to be delivered to all appropriate employees at least annually, tailored to their jobs and risk, and backed by assessments that hold staff accountable. The expectation comes from OFAC's May 2019 Framework for OFAC Compliance Commitments, which names training as the fifth of five essential components of a sanctions compliance program. No statute mandates the training, but OFAC weighs it when deciding penalties.
keyTakeaways: OFAC's Framework (May 2019) lists five essential components of a sanctions compliance program: management commitment, risk assessment, internal controls, testing and auditing, and training.

Training should reach all appropriate employees "at a minimum, annually", give job-specific knowledge, state each employee's sanctions responsibilities, and use assessments to hold employees accountable.

Training scope should match products, customers and geographies; high-risk employees need tailored content; and a confirmed testing or audit deficiency should trigger immediate training or corrective action.

The Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines (31 CFR Part 501, Appendix A) let OFAC mitigate a civil penalty for an effective compliance program, and their annex rates a financial institution's training as low, moderate or high risk.
Since April 24, 2024 the statute of limitations for IEEPA and TWEA sanctions violations is 10 years, and OFAC's recordkeeping period in 31 CFR 501.601 rose to 10 years effective March 12, 2025.
regulator: Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), US Department of the Treasury; federal banking agencies review OFAC compliance in bank examinations
appliesTo: Banks, credit unions, broker-dealers, insurers, money services businesses and other US financial institutions
Any US person, and any organization subject to US jurisdiction
Foreign entities that do business in or with the United States, with US persons, or using US-origin goods or services
Overseas subsidiaries and branches of US organizations, which OFAC's root cause analysis singles out

sections.heading: Where does OFAC's training expectation come from?

blocks.text: It comes from [A Framework for OFAC Compliance Commitments](https://ofac.treasury.gov/media/16331/download?inline), published by OFAC in May 2019, not from a regulation that prescribes training. OFAC sanctions themselves are strict liability prohibitions; the Framework sets out what a risk-based sanctions compliance program (SCP) should contain and how OFAC will treat one in enforcement.

The Framework "strongly encourages" organizations subject to US jurisdiction, and foreign entities dealing with the United States or in US-origin goods or services, to build an SCP on "at least five essential components of compliance: (1) management commitment; (2) risk assessment; (3) internal controls; (4) testing and auditing; and (5) training." OFAC also says that when a civil monetary penalty is warranted, it will decide which of these elements to build into the settlement agreement.

For US financial institutions the expectation has practical force through examinations. The [Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-V/part-501/appendix-Appendix%20A%20to%20Part%20501) in 31 CFR Part 501, Appendix A, let OFAC take into account the views of a firm's federal, state or foreign regulators on its compliance program. Bank examiners generally assess OFAC compliance alongside the Bank Secrecy Act program, which is why many institutions run [BSA/AML training](/regulations/bsa-aml-training-requirements) and sanctions training on one cycle.

sections.heading: What does the Framework say about training?

blocks.text: The Framework expects training for all appropriate employees and personnel at least once a year, with three goals: job-specific knowledge, clear individual responsibilities, and accountability through assessment.

blocks.title: Framework for OFAC Compliance Commitments, Training
blocks.text: "The training program should be provided to all appropriate employees and personnel on a periodic basis (and at a minimum, annually) and generally should accomplish the following: (i) provide job-specific knowledge based on need; (ii) communicate the sanctions compliance responsibilities for each employee; and (iii) hold employees accountable for sanctions compliance training through assessments."
The Framework then lists five commitments an organization makes about training:

items: Training gives adequate information and instruction to employees and, as appropriate, stakeholders such as clients, suppliers, business partners and counterparties, and is further tailored to high-risk employees.
Training scope fits the products and services offered, the customer and partner relationships maintained, and the geographic regions of operation.
Training frequency is appropriate to the OFAC risk assessment and risk profile.
On a confirmed negative testing result, audit finding or other deficiency, the organization takes "immediate and effective action" to train or otherwise correct the relevant personnel.
The program includes easily accessible resources and materials for all applicable personnel.

blocks.text: Two points are easy to miss. First, the annual minimum is a floor; higher-risk roles can justify more frequent training. Second, stakeholders outside the workforce are in scope where appropriate, which matters for correspondent banking, payment processors and agents.

sections.heading: How does OFAC weigh training when it decides penalties?

blocks.text: An effective program, including training, can reduce a penalty and can affect whether a case is treated as egregious. Under General Factor E of the Enforcement Guidelines, OFAC considers "the existence, nature and adequacy of a Subject Person's risk-based OFAC compliance program at the time of the apparent violation", and the Framework says it may mitigate a civil monetary penalty on that basis.

Remediation counts too. Under General Factor F (remedial response), a program built on the five components may earn further mitigation when it leads to corrective steps, which often include targeted retraining. The annex to the Guidelines gives financial institutions a risk matrix with a training row: low risk where training "is appropriate and effective based on the institution's risk profile, covers applicable personnel, and provides necessary up-to-date information"; high risk where training "is sporadic and does not cover important regulatory and risk areas or is nonexistent."

The Framework's appendix lists root causes drawn from past enforcement actions. Several are knowledge failures that training is meant to prevent, including misinterpreting or failing to understand the applicability of OFAC's regulations, improper due diligence on customers' ownership and dealings, sanctions screening software or filter faults, decentralized compliance functions, and individual liability where managers in overseas affiliates facilitated prohibited dealings.

sections.heading: What changed in 2024 and 2025 that affects training records?

blocks.text: The look-back period doubled. The 21st Century Peace through Strength Act, signed on April 24, 2024, extended the statute of limitations for civil and criminal violations of sanctions under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) and the Trading with the Enemy Act (TWEA) from 5 to 10 years, according to OFAC's [interim final rule of September 13, 2024](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/09/13/2024-20674/reporting-procedures-and-penalties).

To match, OFAC amended [31 CFR 501.601](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-V/part-501/subpart-C/section-501.601) so that transaction records must be available for examination for at least 10 years, effective March 12, 2025. The rule covers transaction records, not training records, but an institution that may have to explain a transaction from nine years ago will also want to show what its staff were trained on at the time. Retaining dated training materials, attendance and assessment results for a matching period is a sensible design choice, not a stated OFAC requirement.

sections.heading: How can a financial institution map OFAC training expectations to evidence?

blocks.text: Each Framework commitment translates into a population, a cadence and a record. The mapping below is illustrative; OFAC does not prescribe a format.

blocks.text: Linking each row to the clause it satisfies is the core of [mapping training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations), and the evidence column is what [preparing training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) assembles.

sections.heading: Does OFAC training differ by type of financial institution?

blocks.text: The Framework is the same for every sector, but the content of job-specific training should follow each institution's risk assessment. A bank's highest risks may sit in wire transfers and correspondent accounts; a money transmitter's in agent networks and cross-border corridors; a virtual currency exchanger's in screening counterparties and wallet activity. The AML program rules for [money services businesses](/regulations/fincen-msb-aml-program-training) and [credit unions](/regulations/ncua-credit-union-bsa-training) are separate legal duties, but their training cycles are natural carriers for sanctions content.

Companies facing both sanctions and anti-corruption risk will also see overlap with the Department of Justice's view of training in its [Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs](/regulations/doj-compliance-program-training-expectations). More sector context is on the [financial services industry page](/industries/financial-services).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry starts from the institution's OFAC risk assessment and the Framework's five training commitments, defines what each role must know and how it will be assessed, and only then builds or selects content. Each assessment result and corrective assignment stays linked to the risk and the commitment it addresses, which is the trail OFAC asks for when it evaluates a program.

faqs.q: Is OFAC sanctions training legally mandatory?
faqs.a: No statute or OFAC regulation prescribes sanctions training in the way the Bank Secrecy Act prescribes AML training. OFAC's 2019 Framework strongly encourages it as one of five essential program components, and OFAC considers the program's adequacy when setting penalties. Bank examiners also expect it, so in practice regulated institutions treat it as required.

faqs.q: How often should OFAC training be delivered?
faqs.a: The Framework says training should be provided to all appropriate employees and personnel on a periodic basis "and at a minimum, annually", with frequency appropriate to the institution's OFAC risk assessment and risk profile. Higher-risk roles and staff linked to a deficiency may need more frequent or immediate training.

faqs.q: Does OFAC expect training to include a test?
faqs.a: Yes. One of the three stated goals of the training program is to "hold employees accountable for sanctions compliance training through assessments." A completion record alone does not show that employees understood their responsibilities.

faqs.q: Do non-US companies need OFAC training?
faqs.a: OFAC encourages foreign entities that do business in or with the United States, with US persons, or using US-origin goods or services to adopt a risk-based compliance program, including training. Its root cause analysis highlights violations by non-US persons processing US dollar payments and by overseas affiliates of US companies.

factCheck.claim: Framework lists five essential components: management commitment, risk assessment, internal controls, testing and auditing, training; OFAC 'strongly encourages' organizations subject to US jurisdiction and foreign entities dealing with the US; OCE determines SCP elements for settlements; PDF created May 2, 2019 (US time).

Framework training text: provided to all appropriate employees and personnel periodically 'and at a minimum, annually'; three goals including accountability through assessments; five commitments (stakeholders and high-risk tailoring; scope; frequency; immediate corrective training; accessible resources).

Framework: effective SCP may mitigate CMP under General Factor E and further under General Factor F; may affect egregiousness; appendix root causes include misinterpreting regulations, improper due diligence, screening software faults, decentralized compliance, individual liability.

Enforcement Guidelines General Factor E (compliance program) wording; OFAC may consider views of federal, state or foreign regulators; annex risk matrix training row (low: appropriate and effective; high: sporadic or nonexistent).
